text: Moreover, there is still before the invalid the shock of wonder and delight as he learns he has crossed the indefinable line that separates South from North. This is an uncertain moment—sometimes the awareness comes early, triggered by a simple association: a color, a flower, or a scent; other times, it arrives suddenly one fine morning, when he wakes to southern sunlight streaming through the persiennes and the southern patois faintly audible below. Whether early or late, this pleasure does not end with anticipation, as so many others of the same kind do. It leaves him more awake than he was, and imbues all he sees for days to come with new meaning. There is something in the mere name of the South that carries enthusiasm. At its sound, he sharpens his attention, eager to discover beauty and to memorize the permanent lines and character of the landscape—as if he had been unjustly denied an estate he now claims in full possession. Even those who have never been there before feel as if they have; everyone begins comparing, searching for the familiar, and finding it with ecstatic recognition, as though they were returning home after a long absence, rather than moving farther from it.

Moreover, there is another reason why we are almost inevitably drawn to defend what we believe seriously—because all grotesqueness is intimately tied to seriousness. Unless something is dignified, it cannot be undignified. Why is it funny when a man suddenly sits down in the street? There is only one intelligible answer: that he is the image of God. It’s not funny when anything else falls down—only when a man does. No one finds humor in a tree falling. No one sees absurdity in a stone dropping. No one stops to laugh at snow falling. The fall of thunderbolts is met with gravity; the collapse of roofs or tall buildings is taken seriously. We laugh only when a man tumbles down. Why? Because it is a grave religious event: it is the Fall of Man. Only man can be absurd—because only man can be dignified.

What I narrate was told to me one winter evening by my friend Ah-Yen in the small room behind his laundry. Ah-Yen is a quiet, thoughtful man with a grave and melancholy face—a disposition often seen among his countrymen. Our friendship stretches back several years, and we frequently spend long evenings together in the dimly lit room behind his shop, smoking a dreamy pipe and lost in silent meditation. I am drawn to Ah-Yen chiefly by the highly imaginative nature of his mind, which I believe is a trait common among Eastern people and allows him to escape much of the sordid concerns of his daily work through a rich inner world of his own making. I had no awareness of the sharp, analytical side of his mind until the evening on which I write.

The unfading boyishness of hope and its vigorous irrationality are nowhere more evident than in questions of conduct. There is a character in *The Pilgrim’s Progress*—Mr. Linger-after-Lust—with whom I fancy we are all on speaking terms; one of the most famous for his ingenious hope, sustained even beyond defeat. After eighty years of contrary experience, he still believes it possible to continue in piracy without the guilt of theft. Every sin is our last; every first of January marks a significant turning point in our lives. Any overt act—especially a pledge—is felt to possess alchemical power to transform us. A drunkard takes a vow; it would be strange if that didn’t help. How many years did Mr. Pepys spend making and breaking his small vows? And yet, I’ve never heard that he was ultimately discouraged. By such steps, we try to fix a fleeting resolution—like a timid man rushing to the dentist while the tooth is still aching.

The last inhabitant of these woods before me was an Irishman, Hugh Quoil (though I may have spelled it "coil" too loosely), who lived in Wyman’s tenement—known as Col. Quoil. Rumor said he had been a soldier at Waterloo. If he had lived, I would have made him relive his battles. His trade here was that of a ditcher. Napoleon went to St. Helena; Quoil came to Walden Woods. All I know of him is tragic. He was a man of manners, like someone who had seen the world, and capable of more civil speech than one could easily attend to. In mid-summer, he wore a great coat, affected by a trembling delirium, and his face was the color of carmine. He died on the road at the foot of Brister’s Hill shortly after I arrived, so I never knew him as a neighbor. Before his house was demolished—when his comrades avoided it as “an unlucky castle”—I visited it. There, his old clothes were curled up by use, as if they were himself, upon his raised plank bed. His pipe lay broken on the hearth, not on the fountain, where the bowl had shattered. The latter could never have symbolized his death, for he confessed to me that though he had heard of Brister’s Spring, he had never seen it. Soiled cards—kings of diamonds, spades, and hearts—were scattered across the floor. One black chicken, the administrator could never catch, black as night and silent, not even croaking, still went to roost in the next room. In the rear, there was a dim outline of a garden, planted but never tilled, due to those terrible shaking fits, though it was now harvest time. It was overrun with Roman wormwood and beggar-ticks, the latter clinging to my clothes like fruitless weeds. A woodchuck’s skin was freshly stretched on the back of the house—a trophy from his last Waterloo—but no warm cap or mittens would he have wanted more.

The wildest dreams of wild men, even, are no less true—though they may not appeal to the common sense prevalent among Englishmen and Americans today. Not every truth wins favor with ordinary judgment. Nature has a place for the wild clematis as well as for the cabbage. Some truths are reminiscent; others merely sensible; others prophetic. Some forms of disease may even foreshadow future forms of health. The geologist has found that the shapes of serpents, griffins, flying dragons, and other fanciful heraldic creatures have fossil ancestors—extinct long before humanity existed—suggesting a "faint and shadowy knowledge" of a prior state of organic life. The Hindus dreamed that the earth rests on an elephant, the elephant on a tortoise, and the tortoise on a serpent. Though this may be an unimportant coincidence, it is worth noting that a large fossil tortoise has recently been discovered in Asia—large enough to support an elephant. I confess a fondness for such wild fancies, which transcend time and development. They are the sublimest recreation of the intellect. The partridge loves peas, but not those that go with her into the pot.

I think we may safely trust far more than we currently do. We can afford to neglect just as much care for ourselves as we genuinely give elsewhere. Nature is just as well suited to our weaknesses as to our strengths. The constant anxiety and strain of some people is nearly incurable—almost a disease. We tend to overestimate the importance of the work we do, yet how much of it is actually accomplished? What if we had fallen ill? How vigilant we are! We refuse to live by faith if we can avoid it; we remain on high alert throughout the day, and at night, reluctantly say our prayers, surrendering to uncertainty. We live so thoroughly and sincerely that we reverence our lives and deny the possibility of change. This is the only way we claim, but there are as many paths as there are lines drawn from a single center. All change is a marvel to contemplate—yet it is a miracle happening every instant. Confucius said, “To know that we know what we know, and that we do not know what we do not know, is true knowledge.” When one person brings an imagined fact into clear understanding, I believe eventually all people will build their lives upon that foundation.

As for the kind of audience I enjoy speaking to most, I'd place organizations of sharp, alert business men at the top—such as those found in Boston, New York, Chicago, and Buffalo. I've found no audience more quick to grasp a point or more responsive. In the past few years, I've had the privilege of speaking before most of the leading such organizations in the major U.S. cities. The best time to engage a business audience is after a good dinner—though I consider one of the worst inventions in history the custom requiring a speaker to sit through a fourteen-course meal, every moment certain that their speech will be a failure.

By doing his work, he makes the need he can supply and creates the taste by which he is enjoyed. Through his own work, he unfolds himself. The vice of public speaking is that it lacks abandonment. Somewhere, not only every orator but every man should release all the reins—should find or create a frank, heartfelt expression of the force and meaning within him. The common experience is that a man adjusts as well as he can to the routine details of the work or trade he enters, tending it like a dog turning a spit. Then he becomes part of the machine—he is lost. Until he can communicate himself fully and authentically to others, he has not found his vocation. He must find in that work an outlet for his character, so he may justify it in their eyes. If the labor is mean, let him transform it through thought and character into something liberal. Whatever he knows and thinks, whatever in his awareness is worth doing, let him share it. Otherwise, men will never know him or honor him rightly. It is foolish to accept the meanness and formality of what one does, rather than turning it into an obedient vessel of one’s character and aims.

I wish I could return the affection, but I fear I never will. I have a deep aversion to what they call the "London particular." I feel miserable and muggy on dirty days, and it’s a great relief to take off my clothes and get into bed, out of the way of it all. Everything goes wrong in wet weather. I don’t know why, but it always seems there are more people, dogs, perambulators, cabs, and carts around than at any other time—everyone seems to get in my way, and everybody is so disagreeable, except me. It makes me wildly irritable. And somehow, I always carry more things in wet weather—when I have a bag, three parcels, and a newspaper, a sudden downpour means I can’t open my umbrella.

Before I reached the pond, a new impulse had brought John Field out, with a changed mind, abandoning his "bogging" before sunset. But he, poor man, only disturbed a couple of fins while I was landing a fair string, and he claimed it was his luck. Yet when we switched seats in the boat, luck switched too. Poor John Field—I hope he doesn’t read this, unless it helps him—thinking to live by some outdated country method in this new, primitive land, catching perch with shiners. That can be good bait at times. With his own horizon, yet a poor man, born to poverty, shaped by his inherited Irish hardship, his boggy ways, and his grandmother Adam, he and his descendants will never rise in this world—only their wading, webbed, bog-trotting feet will one day find talaria on their heels.

Except for a few fine works of art, which seem to have appeared by accident, the City of Brussels is like a bad Paris—a Paris in which all the noble elements have been removed and only the unpleasant ones remain. No one can truly understand Paris and its history without recognizing that its fierceness is the balance and justification of its frivolity. It is called a city of pleasure; but it may equally be called a city of pain. The crown of roses is also a crown of thorns. Its people are too ready to hurt others, yet equally willing to hurt themselves. They are martyrs for religion, for irreligion, and even for immorality. The indecency in many of their books and papers is not seductive but horrifying—intended to wound, not to charm. They torture themselves. They use the same whips to stir their own patriotism as they do to silence foreigners. The enemies of France can never describe her infamy or decay with the same force or cruelty as the Nationalists of France describe their own nation. They taunt and torment themselves; at times, they deliberately oppress themselves. Thus, when the Parisian mob could create a government to please itself, it established a form of sublime tyranny—self-governance. The spirit remains unchanged, from the Crusades or St. Bartholomew to the apotheosis of Zola. The old religionists tortured people physically for a moral truth. The new realists torture people morally for a physical truth.

Six months before his death—and nearly a year after he had been struck with paralysis—General Armstrong expressed a wish to visit Tuskegee one last time. Despite having lost the use of his limbs to such an extent that he was practically helpless, his wish was fulfilled, and he was brought to the campus. The owners of the Tuskegee Railroad, white men living in the town, offered to run a special, free train from the main station in Chehaw, five miles away, to meet him. He arrived on the school grounds around nine o’clock in the evening. Someone had suggested a “pine-knot torchlight reception,” and the plan was carried out. As soon as his carriage entered the grounds, he began walking between two lines of lighted, waving pine knots held by over a thousand students and teachers. The scene was so novel and moving that the General was completely overwhelmed with joy. He stayed as a guest in my home for nearly two months. Though almost entirely without voice or mobility, he spent nearly every hour devising ways to help the South. Time and again, he told me that it was not only the duty of the country to uplift the Black people of the South, but also the poor white man. At the end of his visit, I resolved to devote myself even more earnestly than before to the cause that was so close to his heart. I said that if a man in his condition was willing to think, work, and act, then I would do everything possible to fulfill the wishes of his heart.

I, who cannot stay in my chamber a single day without acquiring some rust, and who sometimes ventures out for a walk at the eleventh hour or around four in the afternoon—too late to redeem the day, when the shadows of night have already begun to blend with daylight—have often felt as if I had committed a sin that needs atoning for. I am astonished by the endurance, to say nothing of the moral insensibility, of my neighbors who confine themselves to shops and offices for weeks, months, even years at a time. I cannot fathom what kind of people they are—sitting there at three in the afternoon as if it were three in the morning. Bonaparte may speak of courage at three in the morning, but it is nothing compared to the courage it takes to sit cheerfully at this hour in the afternoon, facing someone you’ve known all morning, and to starve out a garrison to whom you are bound by strong ties of sympathy. I wonder why, between four and five in the afternoon—too late for morning papers and too early for evening ones—there is not a general explosion heard up and down the street, scattering a legion of outdated and homegrown notions and whims to the four winds for airing—and so, the evil cured itself.

This lone leg on which I rest has the simplicity of a Doric column. Architects tell us that a column’s only legitimate purpose is to support weight—and this one fulfills that function. Made of organic, living substance, it may even improve through the process. During these few days of unequal balance, the helplessness or dislocation of one leg might be compensated by the astonishing strength and classic beauty of the other. Mrs. Mountstuart Jenkinson, in Mr. George Meredith’s novel, might pass by at any moment and, seeing me in this stork-like posture, exclaim with equal admiration and literal precision, “He has a leg.” Notice how this famous literary phrase supports my argument about the isolation of any admirable thing. Mrs. Mountstuart Jenkinson, seeking to capture human grace, claimed Sir Willoughby Patterne had a leg. She delicately glossed over the fact that he actually had two—two legs, she deemed, were superfluous, a distraction, a confusion. Two legs would have been like two monuments in London, a clutter of irrelevant details. To have one good leg and another would be to repeat uselessly, like the Gentiles. She would have been just as bewildered as if he had been a centipede.

Hope and the future for me lie not in lawns or cultivated fields, nor in towns and cities, but in the impervious, quaking swamps. When I’ve previously evaluated a farm I considered buying, I’ve often found my attraction centered solely on a few square rods of bog—a natural sink in one corner. That was the jewel that dazzled me. I derive more of my subsistence from the swamps surrounding my native town than from the cultivated gardens in the village. To my eyes, no parterres are richer than the dense beds of dwarf andromeda (Cassandra calyculata) that cover these tender, swampy patches. Botany can only tell me the names of the shrubs there—the high-blueberry, panicled andromeda, lamb-kill, azalea, and rhodora—all standing in the quaking sphagnum. I often wish my house faced this mass of dull red bushes, omitting other flower beds, transplanted spruce, or trim box, even graveled walks. Why not position my house and parlor directly behind this fertile plot, rather than behind that meager collection of curiosities—a poor imitation of nature and art—that I call my front yard? It’s an effort to tidy up after the carpenter and mason have left, done as much for the passer-by as for the resident. The most tasteful front-yard fence has never been pleasing to me; elaborate ornaments—acorn tops or otherwise—soon grow tedious and dull. Bring the sills right up to the edge of the swamp, even if it means a less ideal cellar location, so that no citizens have access from that side. Front yards are not meant to walk in—they are meant to pass through—and you could simply enter from the back.

I notice that it is customary for daily newspapers to publish a column or two of society gossip. They usually head it "Chit-Chat," "On Dit," "Le Boudoir," or something similar, and they fill it with French phrases to give it the right atmosphere. These columns may be interesting in their own way, but I always feel they don’t capture the real essence of what’s going on in our neighbors’ lives. They’re particularly fond of describing events like the delightful dance at Mrs. De Smythe’s—where she looked charming in a gown of old tulle with a stomacher of passementerie—or the dinner party at Mr. Alonzo Robinson’s home, or the smart pink tea given by Miss Carlotta Jones. Those are all pleasant, but they’re not the kind of stories we truly want to hear about. What we’re really interested in are the quiet, everyday scenes of family life—the small details of home life. For instance, take the party at the De Smythes. I’m certain that all who attended would much prefer a brief paragraph describing what happened in their home the morning after the party—a glimpse into the real, unvarnished life of the De Smythes.

We have the same need to grasp a broad view of the world’s religion. We can never truly see Christianity from a catechism—only from the pastures, from a boat in a pond, or amid the songs of woodbirds, if we are lucky. Cleansed by elemental light and wind, and steeped in the sea of beautiful forms the field offers, we might chance upon a brief glance back at biography. Christianity is rightly cherished by the best of humanity. Yet, has there ever been a young philosopher whose education led him into the Christian church without holding Paul’s bold statement especially dear: “Then shall also the Son be subject unto Him who put all things under him, that God may be all in all”? No matter how great or welcome the virtues of individuals may be, the human instinct presses forward toward the impersonal and infinite, and gladly arms itself against the dogmatism of bigots with this generous word from the scripture itself.

Can you remember, reader, when you and I felt something of the same thing? Those glorious days of young manhood—how, coming home along the moonlit road, we felt too alive to walk soberly, and had to spring, skip, wave our arms, and shout until belated farmers' wives thought—and with good reason— that we were mad? We’d stay close to the hedge, laughing aloud as they scuttled off, their blood running cold at our wild parting whoops, and tears would come, though we didn’t know why. Oh, that magnificent young life! It crowned us kings of the earth, surged through every tingling vein, made us feel as if we walked on air, thrilled our throbbing brains, and told us to go forth and conquer the world. It welled up in our young hearts, filling us with a desire to stretch out our arms and gather all the toiling men and women and little children into our embrace and love them all—every one. Ah, those deep, full days, when our future, like an unseen organ, played strange, yearning music in our ears, and our young blood cried out like a war-horse for battle. Ah, our pulse beats slow and steady now, our old joints ache with rheumatism, and we love our easy chair and pipe, sneering at boys’ enthusiasm. But oh, for one brief moment of that god-like life again!

But the union men would not accept "a traitor," the company firmly refused to dismiss such a faithful employee, the busy season had arrived, and everyone involved had finally agreed to abide by the arbitrators’ decision without appeal. The chairman of our small arbitration committee, a venerable judge, quickly showed that trustworthy evidence could not be gathered regarding events now ten years old—the root of this bitterness—and we soon stopped interviewing the conflicting witnesses. The second committee member sternly reminded the men that the oldest Hebraic authority permitted no just resentment to last beyond seven years, and finally, we settled into the painstaking effort to secure the inner consent of all parties—on which, as Maeterlinck has said, the "mystery of justice" ultimately depends. I’m not entirely sure we actually administered justice, but employers, trade-unionists, and arbitrators all agreed that justice in industrial matters must be established with the same care and patience that has long been required in civic life, though, as the judge noted, the search would have little help from precedent. I remain convinced that, no matter how long it takes to establish justice in the new relationships of our raw industrialism, it will never be stable until it has received the sanction of those who bear the heaviest burden of the present situation.

Clinical research shows that moderate coffee consumption is generally benign or mildly beneficial as a stimulant in healthy adults. Ongoing studies explore whether long-term consumption reduces the risk of certain diseases, though some long-term studies have questionable credibility.

The earliest credible evidence of coffee being consumed as a modern beverage comes from Sufi shrines in modern-day Yemen, southern Arabia, in the mid-15th century. There, coffee seeds were roasted and brewed in a way similar to today’s methods. Yemeni growers obtained the beans from the Ethiopian Highlands through coastal Somali intermediaries and began cultivating them. By the 16th century, the drink had spread throughout the Middle East and North Africa, eventually reaching Europe.

The two most commonly grown coffee bean types are C. arabica and C. robusta. Coffee plants are now grown in over 70 countries, mainly in equatorial regions of the Americas, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, and Africa. As of 2018, Brazil was the largest producer, accounting for 35% of the world’s coffee supply. Coffee is a major export commodity and the leading legal agricultural export for many countries. It is one of the most valuable exports from developing nations. Green, unroasted coffee is the most traded agricultural product, and the coffee trade ranks as the second-largest agricultural commodity, behind only petroleum. Despite global sales reaching billions of dollars, farmers who produce the beans often live in poverty. Critics also highlight the industry’s environmental impact, including deforestation for cultivation and high water use. These concerns are driving growth in the fair trade and organic coffee markets.

In the United States, the average size of new single-family homes increased from 1,780 square feet (165 m) in 1978 to 2,479 square feet (230.3 m) in 2007, and further to 2,662 square feet (247.3 m) in 2013. Rising material wealth and higher incomes are commonly cited as reasons for this growth.

The small house movement advocates for homes of less than 1,000 square feet (93 m). The distinction is often made between small homes (400 to 1,000 sq ft or 37 to 93 m) and tiny houses (less than 400 sq ft or 37 m), with some as small as 80 square feet (7.4 m).

Henry David Thoreau and his book *Walden* are frequently cited as early inspiration. Some consider the modern movement to have begun in the 1970s, with artists like Allan Wexler exploring the idea of living in compact spaces. Early pioneers include Lloyd Kahn, author of *Shelter* (1973), and Lester Walker, author of *Tiny Houses* (1987). Sarah Susanka launched the "counter movement" for smaller homes, detailing it in her book *The Not So Big House* (1997).

The tiny-house movement—also known as the "small house movement"—is an architectural and social movement that promotes downsizing living spaces, simplifying life, and essentially "living with less." According to the 2018 International Residential Code, Appendix Q Tiny Houses, a tiny house is defined as a dwelling unit with a maximum floor area of 37 square metres (400 sq ft), excluding lofts. While the movement often reflects a return to simpler living, it is also seen as an eco-friendly alternative to conventional housing and a viable transitional option for people experiencing a lack of shelter.

This distinction is important: many people want to place tiny houses on empty lots, but if a tiny house lacks any essential dwelling amenities, it is classified as an accessory structure and must be located on the same lot as a primary structure, as required by the 2018 International Residential Code. People adopt tiny house living for various reasons. Many reevaluate their values and choose to invest more time in building stronger communities, healing the environment, spending quality time with family, or saving money. Additionally, tiny homes can offer affordable, temporary housing for individuals who have faced a lack of shelter.

Classical board games are divided into four main categories: race games (such as Pachisi), space games (such as Noughts and Crosses), chase games (such as Hnefatafl), and games of displacement (such as chess).

Board games have been played, traveled, and evolved across most cultures and societies throughout history. Important historical sites, artifacts, and documents provide insight into early board games, such as the Jiroft civilization gameboards in Iran. Senet, found in Predynastic and First Dynasty burials in Egypt around 3500 BC and 3100 BC respectively, is the oldest known board game. It appears in a fresco from Merknera’s tomb (3300–2700 BC). Another ancient Egyptian game, Mehen, dates from the predynastic period. Hounds and Jackals, another ancient Egyptian board game, emerged around 2000 BC. The first complete set was discovered in a Theban tomb from the 13th Dynasty. This game was also popular in Mesopotamia and the Caucasus.

Photography is the art, application, and practice of creating durable images by recording light—either electronically using an image sensor or chemically using a light-sensitive material like photographic film. It is widely used in science, manufacturing (e.g., photolithography), and business, as well as in art, film and video production, recreation, hobbies, and mass communication.

Typically, a lens focuses light reflected or emitted from objects into a real image on the light-sensitive surface inside a camera during a timed exposure. With an electronic sensor, this generates an electrical charge at each pixel, which is then processed and stored as a digital image file for display or further use. In photographic emulsion, an invisible latent image is formed, which is later chemically developed into a visible image—either negative or positive—depending on the material and processing method. A negative image on film is traditionally used to produce a positive image on paper, known as a print, either through an enlarger or by contact printing.

Coffee is a brewed drink made from roasted coffee beans, the seeds of berries from certain Coffea species. To become a usable product, the fruit must first be processed—separating the seed from the fruit to produce green coffee. This raw, unroasted coffee is then roasted, a process that transforms it into consumable roasted coffee. Roasted coffee is ground into a powder and mixed with water to make a cup of coffee.

Coffee is dark in color, bitter, slightly acidic, and has a stimulating effect in humans, primarily due to its caffeine content. It is one of the most popular drinks worldwide and can be prepared in many ways—such as espresso, French press, caffè latte, or pre-brewed canned coffee. It is typically served hot, though chilled or iced coffee is also common. Sugar, sugar substitutes, milk, or cream are often added to reduce its bitterness. It is commonly enjoyed with sweet treats like coffee cake or doughnuts. A commercial establishment that sells prepared coffee beverages is known as a coffee shop (not to be confused with Dutch coffeeshops that sell cannabis).

There is debate about the historical accuracy of this legend. The Greek historian Herodotus, the primary source for the Greco-Persian Wars, mentions Philippides as the messenger who ran from Athens to Sparta to request help, and then returned—covering a distance of over 240 kilometres (150 mi) each way. In some manuscripts of Herodotus, the runner between Athens and Sparta is named Philippides. However, Herodotus makes no mention of a messenger sent from Marathon to Athens. Instead, he states that the main Athenian army, having fought and won the grueling battle, feared a naval attack by the Persian fleet on an undefended Athens and marched quickly back to the city, arriving the same day.

In 1879, Robert Browning wrote the poem *Pheidippides*. His composite story became part of late 19th-century popular culture and was widely accepted as a historical fact.

Mount Pentelicus lies between Marathon and Athens, meaning that if Philippides actually made the famous run after the battle, he would have had to circumvent the mountain—either to the north or south. The southern route, the more direct and obvious path, closely follows the modern Marathon-Athens highway. This route runs south from Marathon Bay along the coast, then gradually climbs westward toward the eastern edge of Athens, between the foothills of Mount Hymettus and Mount Penteli, before descending into Athens. When the Olympics were revived in 1896, this route was about 40 kilometres (25 mi) long and was the distance used for the original marathon race. However, some suggest Philippides may have taken an alternative path: a westward climb up the eastern and northern slopes of Mount Penteli to the pass of Dionysos, followed by a straight southward descent to Athens. This route is slightly shorter—about 35 kilometres (22 mi)—but involves a steep initial ascent of over 5 kilometres (3.1 mi).

In medieval kitchen gardens, vegetable plants such as fennel, cabbage, onion, garlic, leeks, radishes, parsnips, peas, lentils, and beans were grown whenever space allowed. Gillyflowers were also cultivated in containers.

During the Renaissance, plant collectors and wealthy merchants from Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium imported plants from Asia Minor and the East Indies. Senecio angulatus was introduced to Malta and much of Europe in the 15th century as an ornamental plant. In the 16th century, fascination with exotic plants grew among the aristocracy of France and England. Though Sir Hugh Platt’s *Garden of Eden* was published in 1660—after the 16th century—it reflected the growing interest in cultivating plants in homes.

Until the 17th century, there was little evidence of a houseplant culture in Central Europe. One possible explanation is the low standard of living at the time. Using a window sill in the living room as a plant shelter offered limited light, restricted storage, and reduced freedom of movement. Even in often dark and unheated side rooms, plants were rare.

Younger students who spend more time on homework tend to have slightly worse or the same academic performance as those who spend less time. Homework has not been shown to improve academic achievement in grade school. Proponents argue that assigning homework to young children helps develop good study habits, suggesting that doing potentially unnecessary homework from ages five to ten prepares them for necessary homework from ages 10 to 15. However, no research has ever been conducted to verify whether this claim holds any merit.

Among teenagers, students who spend somewhat more time on homework generally have higher grades and better test scores than those who spend less time. That said, large amounts of homework can lead to declining academic performance, even among older students. While students assigned homework in middle and high school tend to score slightly better on standardized tests, those who have more than 90 minutes of homework daily in middle school or more than two hours in high school perform worse.

Organized chess emerged in the 19th century, and today is governed internationally by FIDE (International Chess Federation). The first universally recognized World Chess Champion, Wilhelm Steinitz, claimed the title in 1886; Magnus Carlsen is the current champion. A vast body of chess theory has developed since the game's inception. Elements of art are evident in chess composition, and chess has influenced Western culture and art, with connections to fields such as mathematics, computer science, and psychology.

One of the early goals of computer scientists was to build a chess-playing machine. In 1997, Deep Blue became the first computer to defeat the reigning World Champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match. Today’s chess engines are far stronger than even the best human players and have profoundly shaped the development of chess theory.

The official rules of chess are published by FIDE (Fédération Internationale des Échecs) in its Handbook. Rules issued by national bodies or unaffiliated organizations, commercial publishers, and others may vary in minor details. FIDE’s rules were most recently updated in 2018.

A newspaper is a periodical publication that contains written information about current events, typically printed in black ink on a white or gray background.

Newspapers cover a wide range of topics, including politics, business, sports, and art. They often include opinion columns, weather forecasts, reviews of local services, obituaries, birth notices, crosswords, editorial cartoons, comic strips, and advice columns.

Most newspapers are businesses that fund their operations through subscriptions, newsstand sales, and advertising. The journalism organizations that publish them are often referred to metonymically as newspapers.

Traditionally, newspapers were printed on cheap, low-grade paper known as newsprint. Today, most are also available online as digital publications, and some have completely discontinued their print editions.

Newspapers originated in the 17th century as information sheets for merchants. By the early 19th century, many cities across Europe, as well as in North and South America, had established newspaper publications.

In 1881, Charles Fritts created the first commercial solar panel, which he reported as producing "continuous, constant, and considerable force—not only from direct sunlight but also from dim, diffused daylight." However, these panels were extremely inefficient, especially when compared to coal-fired power plants. In 1939, Russell Ohl developed the solar cell design now used in many modern panels, which he patented in 1941. In 1954, Bell Labs first used this design to create the first commercially viable silicon solar cell. In 1957, Mohamed M. Atalla at Bell Labs developed the process of silicon surface passivation through thermal oxidation—a technique now critical to improving solar cell efficiency.

Photovoltaic modules convert sunlight (photons) into electricity via the photovoltaic effect. Most modules use either wafer-based crystalline silicon cells or thin-film cells. The structural (load-bearing) component of a module can be either the top or back layer. Cells must be protected from mechanical damage and moisture. Most modules are rigid, though semi-flexible versions based on thin-film cells are also available. Cells are typically connected electrically in series to achieve the desired voltage and in parallel to increase current. The power output (in watts) of a module is the product of its voltage (in volts) and current (in amps). Manufacturer specifications are provided under standard test conditions, which do not reflect the actual operating environment of solar panels on a site.

Recyclable materials include many types of glass, paper, cardboard, metal, plastic, tires, textiles, batteries, and electronics. The composting or other reuse of biodegradable waste—such as food or garden waste—is also considered a form of recycling. Materials are typically delivered to a household recycling center or picked up from curbside bins, then sorted, cleaned, and reprocessed into new materials for use in manufacturing products.

In the strictest sense, recycling produces a fresh supply of the same material—for example, used office paper becoming new office paper, or used polystyrene foam becoming new polystyrene. This ideal is achieved when materials like metal cans are recycled repeatedly, indefinitely, without losing purity. However, this is often difficult or too expensive compared to producing the material from raw sources, so recycling many products typically involves reusing the material in different forms (such as turning paper into paperboard). Another form of recycling is the recovery of valuable or hazardous materials from complex products—for instance, extracting lead from car batteries or gold from printed circuit boards, or removing mercury from thermometers and thermostats.

Telecommuting—also known as remote working, telework, teleworking, working from home (WFH), mobile work, remote job, work from anywhere (WFA), or flexible workplace—is a work arrangement in which employees do not commute or travel (e.g., by bus, bicycle, or car) to a central workplace such as an office building, warehouse, or store.

In the 1990s, telecommuting gained attention in popular culture. In 1995, the phrase "work is something you do, not something you travel to" was coined. Variations include: "Work is something we DO, not a place that we GO" and "Work is what we do, not where we are." A wide range of businesses, governments, and nonprofit organizations have adopted telecommuting. Companies use it to reduce costs—telecommuting employees don’t need office space or cubicles, which eliminates expenses for rent, lighting, climate control, and other overhead. It also improves workers’ quality of life by reducing commuting time and traffic congestion. Teleworking can help employees better balance work and personal responsibilities, such as caring for children or elderly parents. Additionally, some organizations adopt remote work for environmental reasons, as it reduces road congestion and air pollution by decreasing the number of vehicles on the road.

Beekeeping, or apiculture, involves the maintenance of bee colonies—typically in man-made hives—by humans. Most of these bees are honey bees in the genus Apis, though other honey-producing species, such as stingless Melipona bees, are also kept. A beekeeper, or apiarist, raises bees to harvest honey and other hive products like beeswax, propolis, flower pollen, bee pollen, and royal jelly, to pollinate crops, or to produce bees for sale to other beekeepers. A location where bees are kept is known as an apiary or "bee yard."

Depictions of humans gathering honey from wild bees date back to 10,000 years ago. Beekeeping in pottery vessels began around 9,000 years ago in North Africa. Evidence of bee domestication appears in Egyptian art from about 4,500 years ago. Early beekeepers used simple hives and smoke, storing honey in jars—some of which were found in the tombs of pharaohs like Tutankhamun. It wasn't until the 18th century that European understanding of bee colonies and their biology enabled the development of the movable-comb hive, allowing honey to be harvested without destroying the entire colony.

In North America, many birders distinguish themselves from birdwatchers, and the term "birder" is unfamiliar to most laypeople. At its most basic, the distinction is seen as one of dedication or intensity—though this is subjective. Self-described birders typically feel more knowledgeable about detailed aspects like identification (visual and aural), molt, distribution, migration timing, and habitat use. While these dedicated birders may travel specifically to see birds, birdwatchers are sometimes described as having a more limited scope, perhaps staying close to their own yards or local parks. Indeed, in 1969, a Birding Glossary published in Birding magazine defined:

Bird-watcher: A somewhat ambiguous term for anyone who observes birds for any reason; it should not be used to refer to a serious birder.

Twitching—a British term—refers to the pursuit of a previously located rare bird. In North America, it is more commonly called "chasing." The term "twitcher" is sometimes incorrectly used as a synonym for birder, but it specifically refers to those who travel long distances to see a rare bird, which is then added to their list. The term originated in the 1950s, referring to the nervous behavior of British birdwatcher Howard Medhurst. Earlier terms for such individuals included pot-hunter, tally-hunter, or tick-hunter. The primary goal of twitching is often to build up species on one’s list. Some birders engage in competition to achieve the longest list. The act of pursuing a rare bird is called a twitch or a chase. A rare bird that remains long enough to be seen is described as twitchable or chaseable.

The word "photography" is derived from the Greek roots φωτός (phōto's), the genitive of φῶς (phōs), meaning "light," and γραφή (graphé), meaning "representation by means of lines" or "drawing," together forming the phrase "drawing with light."

Several individuals may have independently created the term from these roots. Hercules Florence, a French painter and inventor living in Campinas, Brazil, used the French form, photographie, in private notes believed to have been written as early as 1834. While this claim is widely reported, it has not yet gained broad international recognition. The first known public use of the term by the Franco-Brazilian inventor came to wider attention following Boris Kossoy’s research in 1980.

The German newspaper Vossische Zeitung, on 25 February 1839, published an article entitled *Photographie*, discussing various priority claims—particularly Henry Fox Talbot's—regarding Daguerre's claim of invention. This article marks the earliest known public appearance of the word. It was signed "J.M.," believed to be Berlin astronomer Johann von Maedler. Sir John Herschel is also credited with independently coining the term in 1839, separate from Talbot.

Volunteering is a voluntary act in which individuals or groups freely give their time and labor for community service. Many volunteers are specifically trained in fields such as medicine, education, or emergency rescue, while others serve as needed—such as in response to a natural disaster.

The word was first recorded in 1755, derived from the noun *volunteer*, which dates to around 1600 as "one who offers himself for military service," from Middle French *voluntaire*. In its non-military sense, the term was first used in the 1630s. The phrase *volunteering* gained more recent usage—still largely tied to military contexts—alongside the concept of *community service*. In a military setting, a volunteer army consists of soldiers who choose to serve rather than being conscripted. These volunteers are not working for free; they receive regular pay.

During this period, America experienced the Great Awakening, a time when people became more aware of social injustices and began advocating against slavery. In 1851, the first YMCA in the United States was established, followed seven years later by the first YWCA. During the American Civil War, women volunteered to sew supplies for soldiers, and Clara Barton, known as the "Angel of the Battlefield," led a team providing aid to servicemen. Barton founded the American Red Cross in 1881 and began organizing volunteers for disaster relief, including assistance after the Johnstown Flood in 1889.

Bread is a staple food made from a dough of flour and water, typically baked. Throughout recorded history, it has been a central part of diets in many parts of the world. One of the oldest human-made foods, bread has been vital since the beginning of agriculture and continues to play a key role in both religious rituals and everyday culture.

Bread can be leavened using naturally occurring microbes, chemicals, industrially produced yeast, or high-pressure aeration. In many countries, commercial bread includes additives to enhance flavor, texture, color, shelf life, nutrition, and ease of production.

The Old English word for bread was *hlaf* (hlaifs in Gothic, modern English *loaf*), which appears to be the oldest Teutonic term. Old High German *hleib* and modern German *Laib* stem from this Proto-Germanic root, which was borrowed into some Slavic languages (e.g., Czech *chléb*, Polish *bochen chleba*, Russian *khleb*) and Finnic languages (e.g., Finnish *leipä*, Estonian *leib*). The Middle and Modern English word *bread* is found in various Germanic languages, such as West Frisian *brea*, Dutch *brood*, German *Brot*, Swedish *bröd*, and Norwegian and Danish *brød*; it may be related to *brew* or perhaps to *break*, originally meaning "broken piece" or "morsel."

Board games are tabletop games that typically involve pieces moved or placed on a pre-marked board (playing surface), and often incorporate elements of table, card, role-playing, and miniatures games.

Most feature competition between two or more players. In checkers, a player wins by capturing all opposing pieces, while Eurogames often conclude with a final score calculation. Pandemic is a cooperative game where all players win or lose as a team, and peg solitaire is a solo puzzle.

There are many varieties of board games. Their representation of real-life situations can range from themeless, like checkers, to those with a specific theme and narrative, such as Cluedo. Rules can range from simple—like in Snakes and Ladders—to deeply complex, as in Advanced Squad Leader.

The time needed to learn or master a game varies widely, but is not necessarily tied to the number or complexity of rules. Games like chess or Go have relatively simple rule sets but offer deep strategic play.
